title: Creativity Lives in Constraints
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien argues that creativity is not a gift that flourishes in open-ended freedom but a response to limits. Open briefs overwhelm people with decisions, whereas even professional creatives begin from a core constraint and build outward. He illustrates the point with a game of human Pong played with a colleague during exam supervision, the tiny memory budget of Super Mario Bros, Taskmaster tasks and the bottle episode of Community. He then turns to schools, criticising professional learning sessions that dump a dozen strategies on staff with no clear call to action, and an English team that let students use AI to generate story ideas they lack the background knowledge to write about. His practical conclusion is to give students a limited set of topics to explore in depth and to treat time pressure and curriculum requirements as constraints that can spur innovation.
points: Open-ended creative tasks create decision paralysis, so a well-chosen constraint is often what makes a good idea possible.
Professional learning that delivers many strategies with no clear next step overloads staff and typically changes nothing.
Letting students use AI to generate ideas for creative writing risks surface-level work and invites them to outsource the whole piece, because they lack the knowledge to develop the ideas.
Offering students a short menu of topics to explore deeply is likely to produce stronger writing than a blank page.
Constraints such as deadlines or a curriculum point you dislike can prompt teachers to innovate, as the author found when rebuilding his resources for teaching the Constitution.
quotes: Open-ended tasks can be incredibly challenging for the limitless decisions they create and the inability to know which idea is the best one to go with.

Even creatives rarely sit down and just wait for any idea to come to them. Many will start with a core idea in mind and then begin to flesh out the idea based on that core constraint they set about themselves.

Suddenly, you have staff with a dozen strategies that they could potentially try in a myriad of different ways and the mental load of all the possible combinations and outcomes leads to nothing changing.
This creativity did not come from endless options. It came from constraints. All we could do was walk. We couldn’t leave the room.

the moment you open up AI for the idea generation of young people who are still developing their ability to make wise decisions, you are likely inviting those same students to try and get away with having AI write the whole piece.
Setting those students a limited amount of topics to start with to choose from that they could then explore in more depth is likely to lead to far more high quality attempts at writing.
If you’ve ever been the person who can suddenly write the essay or assignment of your life the night before it’s due, then you too have benefited from constraints igniting your creativity.
